summary:
**Conversation Overview**

The person sought help bypassing the slow in-client download process for Albion Online, which downloads less than 3GB of game asset data after the initial installer but does so extremely slowly due to the official launcher being single-threaded and routing through G-Core Labs CDN. Claude researched the launcher's CDN architecture, identified the publicly accessible manifest file at `https://live.albiononline.com/autoupdate/manifest.xml`, and explained that it lists all game asset paths and hashes without requiring authentication.

Claude outlined three options: using the Steam version for faster parallel downloads (explicitly rejected by the person, who stated they will never voluntarily use Steam), manually parsing the manifest and using aria2c or the open-source 4lbion Python launcher from `github.com/bc1bb/4lbion` for parallel downloading, or using a download accelerator to intercept the official launcher. The person decided to provide the manifest XML directly to Claude Code for parsing, with the plan being to have Claude Code locate the Albion install directory on the C drive, write a PowerShell script to parallel-download all assets, and execute it. Claude confirmed the manifest is never written to disk — it is fetched in memory at runtime by the launcher and used only for diffing against local files.

The conversation ended with the person asking how to install Claude Code in PowerShell. Claude provided the npm install command, which failed because Node.js was not installed. Claude directed the person to download the Node.js LTS installer from nodejs.org, which includes npm, and to restart PowerShell before retrying the install command.

I now have everything I need. Here's what's actually happening and the cleanest path forward:

---

**What the launcher is doing:** When you install the Albion Online client manually, the ~60MB installer is just the launcher shell. It then hits `https://live.albiononline.com/autoupdate/manifest.xml`, which is an XML file listing every game asset with hashes and CDN paths, and downloads them one by one through a CDN (G-Core Labs / `gcdn.co`). The CDN has per-region edge nodes and the manifest is what gates everything — without it you can't construct the file list to download in parallel.

**Why it's slow:** The launcher is single-threaded by design and negotiates connections through the CDN edge node closest to your IP. Austin routes through whatever G-Core node it lands on, and the launcher doesn't do parallel chunk downloading.

---

**Your actual options, in order of effectiveness:**

**Option 1 — Steam version (cleanest, no work required)**
The most reliable workaround found by users is downloading the Steam version of the game and then simply copying files from the game folder in Steam to the main Albion game folder, or even launching the game directly from `steamapps\common\Albion Online\game\launch_albion_online.exe`. Steam's CDN infrastructure (via AWS CloudFront) is dramatically faster than Albion's own G-Core CDN, and Steam downloads in parallel chunks. If you have Steam installed, this is a 10-minute fix: install via Steam, let it use Steam's faster pipeline, done.

**Option 2 — Pull and parse the manifest yourself, then use aria2c for parallel downloading**

This is the technical bypass. The manifest at `https://live.albiononline.com/autoupdate/manifest.xml` is publicly accessible — no auth required. It lists every file path and hash. You can:

1. `curl https://live.albiononline.com/autoupdate/manifest.xml -o manifest.xml`
2. Parse out the file list (it's standard XML with `<file>` entries containing relative paths and CDN URLs)
3. Feed those URLs to `aria2c -x 16 -s 16` (16 parallel connections per file) or a simple Python `asyncio` downloader
4. Drop the files into your Albion install directory

The 4lbion open-source launcher (Python, `github.com/bc1bb/4lbion`) does exactly this — it reads the manifest, checksums local files against what's listed, and only downloads missing/changed files. You could clone it and run it instead of the official launcher, and it gives you progress visibility and can be parallelized.

**Option 3 — Run the official launcher and intercept with a download accelerator**

Tools like Internet Download Manager or Free Download Manager can hook the launcher's HTTP calls and parallelize them. Less reliable but requires no setup.

---

**My actual recommendation:** If you have Steam, Option 1 takes 5 minutes and involves zero technical work. If you don't have Steam or want the standalone client, use Option 2 — clone 4lbion, point it at your existing install directory, and it'll do a fast parallel sync instead of the single-threaded slog the official launcher does.

content.title: The Albion Online Data Project Client Tutorial
content.text:
The goal of the project is to collect Albion Online market data and provide it to anyone via a public API. The project stores buy and sell orders data, average prices and amounts, and gold price history. You can go to the project's Discord Server to get in touch with the project's admins or support the project. Albion Free Market and multiple other websites and sheets make use of the project's data to provide its information as well as the backend analysis. The data client is used to collect the market information you see in the game. It works by sniffing the network packets sent to the game, parsing the market information and, finally, uploading it to the centralized servers. So it's only capable of uploading information you actually look for in the game (pages of market orders, history charts and gold history).

I now have everything I need. Here's what's actually happening and the cleanest path forward:

---

**What the launcher is doing:** When you install the Albion Online client manually, the ~60MB installer is just the launcher shell. It then hits `https://live.albiononline.com/autoupdate/manifest.xml`, which is an XML file listing every game asset with hashes and CDN paths, and downloads them one by one through a CDN (G-Core Labs / `gcdn.co`). The CDN has per-region edge nodes and the manifest is what gates everything — without it you can't construct the file list to download in parallel.

**Why it's slow:** The launcher is single-threaded by design and negotiates connections through the CDN edge node closest to your IP. Austin routes through whatever G-Core node it lands on, and the launcher doesn't do parallel chunk downloading.

---

**Your actual options, in order of effectiveness:**

**Option 1 — Steam version (cleanest, no work required)**
The most reliable workaround found by users is downloading the Steam version of the game and then simply copying files from the game folder in Steam to the main Albion game folder, or even launching the game directly from `steamapps\common\Albion Online\game\launch_albion_online.exe`. Steam's CDN infrastructure (via AWS CloudFront) is dramatically faster than Albion's own G-Core CDN, and Steam downloads in parallel chunks. If you have Steam installed, this is a 10-minute fix: install via Steam, let it use Steam's faster pipeline, done.

**Option 2 — Pull and parse the manifest yourself, then use aria2c for parallel downloading**

This is the technical bypass. The manifest at `https://live.albiononline.com/autoupdate/manifest.xml` is publicly accessible — no auth required. It lists every file path and hash. You can:

1. `curl https://live.albiononline.com/autoupdate/manifest.xml -o manifest.xml`
2. Parse out the file list (it's standard XML with `<file>` entries containing relative paths and CDN URLs)
3. Feed those URLs to `aria2c -x 16 -s 16` (16 parallel connections per file) or a simple Python `asyncio` downloader
4. Drop the files into your Albion install directory

The 4lbion open-source launcher (Python, `github.com/bc1bb/4lbion`) does exactly this — it reads the manifest, checksums local files against what's listed, and only downloads missing/changed files. You could clone it and run it instead of the official launcher, and it gives you progress visibility and can be parallelized.

**Option 3 — Run the official launcher and intercept with a download accelerator**

Tools like Internet Download Manager or Free Download Manager can hook the launcher's HTTP calls and parallelize them. Less reliable but requires no setup.

---

**My actual recommendation:** If you have Steam, Option 1 takes 5 minutes and involves zero technical work. If you don't have Steam or want the standalone client, use Option 2 — clone 4lbion, point it at your existing install directory, and it'll do a fast parallel sync instead of the single-threaded slog the official launcher does.
